# E-1899 — Remove the unused list tree

A removal checklist, not a design. The only risk in this task is deleting the
wrong `--tree`: there are four flags by that name and two identically-named
glyph maps, and the two flags you must NOT touch are the ones actually in use.

> **Amended during implementation.** Three things landed that this plan did not
> anticipate; each is marked ⊕ below.
>
> 1. A **third bare `tree` reference** in `show_plan` — the sort default —
>    which the site table missed. Mechanical.
> 2. A **doc line** in `docs/guide/tasks.md` advertising the removed flag.
> 3. The **second `status_indicators` map was deleted too**, reversing this
>    plan's "Do NOT touch" directive. It turned out to be dead code. See
>    *Reversal* below; filed and closed as E-1924.

## One renderer, two flags

`epic_cmd.list_epics` is a thin wrapper that forwards `tree=tree` into
`task_cmd.show_plan` with `type_filter="epic"`. So `task list --tree` and
`epic list --tree` share a single implementation — there is ONE branch and ONE
glyph map to delete, not two.

## Remove

| Site | What |
|---|---|
| `cli.py:1225` | the `--tree/as_tree` option on `task list` |
| `cli.py:2521` | the `--tree/as_tree` option on `epic list` |
| `cli.py` (both bodies) | the `tree=as_tree` argument passed onward |
| `epic_cmd.list_epics` | the `tree` parameter and its pass-through to `show_plan` |
| `task_cmd.show_plan` | the `tree` parameter |
| `task_cmd.show_plan` | the `else: # Tree output` branch — the `by_id` / `children_of` / `_render` block, ending at the `_render(None, 1)` call |
| `task_cmd.py` ~:1100 | the `status_indicators` map that opens that branch |
| ⊕ `task_cmd.show_plan` | the sort default `if not tree and not sort_by:` → `if not sort_by:` |
| ⊕ `docs/guide/tasks.md:34` | the `endless task list --tree # hierarchical` line |
| ⊕ `task_cmd.next_tasks` ~:1209 | the second `status_indicators` map — see *Reversal* |

After removal, `show_plan`'s `if not tree: _render_flat_table(rows)` collapses
to an unconditional `_render_flat_table(rows)`; the trailing `click.echo()` and
the `N item(s)` summary below the branch stay.

⊕ The site table above missed a third bare `tree` reference: `show_plan` picked
its ORDER BY with `if not tree and not sort_by: sort_by = "id"`, falling through
to `pi.sort_order` for the tree. Removing the parameter leaves `if not sort_by`.
Flat ordering is unchanged — the flat path always defaulted to id. A `NameError`
on the first `task list` after the branch deletion is what surfaced it.

## ⊕ Reversal — the second glyph map went too

This plan told the implementer to preserve the `status_indicators` map in
`next_tasks` as an unrelated bystander. That was wrong: the map is **dead
code**. It is assigned and never read — `next_tasks` renders through
`_render_flat_table`, which has no glyph column. `grep -n 'indicator'
task_cmd.py` returned only the assignment line.

So the resolution is deletion, not preservation. Adding a glyph column to
`task next` to make the map live would be an unrequested behavior change;
`task next` output is byte-for-byte what it was. Filed as E-1924
(`cleans_up` E-1899), then folded into this task's commit and closed obsolete.

Consequence for the framing at the top of this plan: there were two
identically-named glyph maps and **both** are gone. The "don't delete the wrong
one" hazard is now only about the four `--tree` flags.

## Do NOT touch

- **`session status --tree`** (`cli.py:815`) and **`session monitor --tree`**
  (`cli.py:839`). These are the trees actually in use. They are Go-backed
  (`internal/sessionstatuscmd`), reach the renderer through
  `session_status_resolve`, and share nothing with the list tree but the flag
  name.

## Verification — `tests/tasks/e-1899-verify.sh`

Author the script; it is the deliverable the user runs. Hand back exactly one
command:

```
esu && ./tests/tasks/e-1899-verify.sh
```

Copy the harness shape from `tests/tasks/e-1845-verify.sh` (the `report_pass` /
`report_fail` / `assert_*` / `summary` block and the isolated-fixture setup:
throwaway git repo, temp `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`/`XDG_CACHE_HOME`, worktree `bin` on
PATH). E-1623 will retrofit these onto a shared harness later; until then match
the current shape rather than inventing a new one.

**A — fail-fast gate.** `uv run pytest tests/ -q` passes. A removal must not
break an unrelated suite, and there is no point running the rest if it did.
Abort the run on failure.

**B — the flags are gone.** `endless task list --tree` and
`endless epic list --tree` both fail as unknown options, and their `--help`
output no longer lists `--tree`.

**C — the flat table is untouched.** `endless task list` and
`endless epic list` still render, and `--status`, `--phase`, `--sort`, `--llm`,
and `--json` all still behave. Seed a small task tree with parents and children
so a regression in the flat renderer would actually show.

**D — the trees that matter still work.** `endless session status --tree` and
`endless session monitor --tree` still render. This is the check that catches
the one dangerous failure mode of this task: deleting the wrong `--tree`. Assert
against real output, not just an exit code.

**E — ⊕ both glyph maps are gone and `task next` is unchanged.** As written this
check asserted that `endless task next` "still renders its status glyphs" —
a false premise: it never rendered them, which is exactly how the map was found
to be dead. Reframed to the guarantee that actually holds: no `status_indicators`
survives in `task_cmd.py`, nothing reads an `indicator`, and `task next` still
renders its header, column heads, rows, `--json` and `--llm` exactly as before.

**F — no dangling references.** Grep the tree for `tree=` and `as_tree` in
`src/endless`; the only survivors should be the two `session_status_resolve`
call sites. Nothing should still pass `tree` to `show_plan` or `list_epics`.

**⊕ G — project-wide regression.** `go test ./...` passes. The Python suite is
already the section-A gate; this is its Go counterpart, run at the end.

## Not in scope

An interactive TUI tree — what is actually wanted instead of this — is a much
larger piece of work and is deliberately unfiled.

## Note for E-1891

The deleted glyph map is the per-row lookup cited in E-1891's plan as the one
place worth measuring for subprocess cost. Landing this first dissolves that
concern rather than answering it. ⊕ Doubly so: both maps are now gone, so
whichever of the two E-1891 meant, there is nothing left to measure.

# Plan — E-1893: require replies to restate the task IDs they are about

## Decisions (user, 2026-08-08)

Delivery surfaces: **handoff templates, the E-1919 output style, and `endless guide`**.
Explicitly NOT the E-1803 PostToolUse nudge — E-1911 just rewrote that nudge and parked
E-1901's enforcement arm, so it is recently-settled ground this task will not disturb.

The style's reach gap is closed two ways: activate it for endless now, and add a
**dim FYI on stderr** telling a *human* operator the style is installed but inactive.
Optional in principle; treated as required for any project using Endless for now.

## Part 1 — handoff templates (one sentence, one place)

The analysis's open question (a line in each of seven templates vs a shared fragment)
resolves itself: `internal/templatecmd/templates/handoff/_close.tmpl` already exists,
already holds the reporting instructions, and is already parsed into every handoff
template's set via `handoffPartialNames`. Add the rule to the `handoff_close` define.

Wording must cover the crux from the analysis — the subject is often NOT the session's
own task, so the tmux window title does not supply the missing ID:

> Name the explicit task ID(s) in the first sentence that makes a claim about a task —
> including tasks other than your own, where my window title tells me nothing.

Do NOT add it to `handoff_verify` / `handoff_nonverify`; those are about the verify
command, and duplicating the rule invites drift between copies.

## Part 2 — E-1919 output style

The style's `## Lead with the IDs` section already says to open with the bare
identifiers the answer concerns. It does not stress the other-tasks case, which the
analysis calls the crux. Strengthen that section only — do not restructure it.

Because the style file is embedded, the change is made in
`internal/outputstylecmd/templates/Endless.md.tmpl`, then re-materialized into
`.claude/output-styles/Endless.md` with `outputstyle install --force`. Both copies must
be committed; a stale committed copy would silently shadow the intent.

`tests/tasks/e-1919-verify.sh` section 8 asserts the style body's contract clauses. Add
an assertion for the other-tasks wording so this cannot regress.

## Part 3 — `endless guide`

Add the rule to the reporting guidance in the guide's orchestration/reporting section,
for sessions not started from a handoff. Keep it to the same one sentence used in
`_close.tmpl` — three surfaces carrying three paraphrases is how the rule drifts.

Re-run `just regenerate-guide` if the section map changes.

## Part 4 — activate the style for endless

Commit `"outputStyle": "Endless"` into the main checkout's tracked
`.claude/settings.json`. Verified safe: `just claude-settings-init` rebuilds each
worktree's settings from the committed copy's non-hook keys plus the working copy's,
replacing only `hooks` (justfile:381-385), so the key survives worktree regeneration
rather than being dropped.

Note this is a genuine behavior change for every endless session, which is why E-1919
made it opt-in. It is being opted into deliberately here, not by default.

## Part 5 — the dim FYI (human-only, stderr, appended)

**Trigger:** any `endless` command run by a human. Never when run by an agent.

**Detection already exists — twice.** `agent_help.is_claude_code_agent()` and
`task_cmd._running_under_agent()` are byte-identical (`CLAUDECODE == "1"`). Consolidate
onto `agent_help.is_claude_code_agent()` and delete the duplicate rather than adding a
third caller — same reasoning that folded `templatecmd` onto
`monitor.ProjectRootFromCwd` in E-1919.

**Behavior:**
- Fires only when `not is_claude_code_agent()`.
- Fires only when the project has the style file present but `outputStyle` unset (or set
  to something else) in `.claude/settings.json` — i.e. exactly the inert state
  `outputstyle install` warns about.
- Writes to **stderr**, dim, appended after the command's normal output, so it never
  corrupts stdout for pipes/`--json` consumers.
- One line. Not an error, not a non-zero exit.
- Suppressed when the project has no style file at all (nothing to activate) and when
  `.claude/settings.json` is unreadable.

**Wording:** dim, and it must name the activation route, since there is no
`/output-style` command:

> FYI: the Endless output style is installed but not active — `/config output-style=Endless`

**Throttle:** must not print on every command in a tight loop. Reuse the existing
activity-throttle shape (`monitor.ShouldThrottle`) or an equivalent once-per-N-minutes
marker under the cache dir. Decide at implementation time; do NOT ship an unthrottled
per-invocation nag — that is the noise failure that got E-1901's gate parked.

**Placement:** a single hook in the Python CLI's result callback / group teardown so it
appends after any subcommand, rather than being pasted into individual commands.

## Verification

Fold into the existing suite per the one-command rule:
`esu && ./tests/tasks/e-1893-verify.sh`

Checks:
1. `handoff_close` renders the ID rule for every handoff type (todo, bugfix, research,
   epic, brainstorm, respawn) — asserts the shared partial actually reaches all of them.
2. The rule appears exactly once per rendered handoff, not once per template that
   includes a partial.
3. The style body carries the other-tasks wording.
4. The embedded template and the committed `.claude/output-styles/Endless.md` are
   byte-identical — catches a re-materialization that was forgotten.
5. `endless guide` output contains the rule.
6. The FYI fires with `CLAUDECODE` unset and a project in the inert state.
7. The FYI does NOT fire when `CLAUDECODE=1`.
8. The FYI does NOT fire when `outputStyle` is already `Endless`.
9. The FYI goes to stderr, not stdout: stdout of a `--json` command still parses.
10. The FYI does not change exit status.
11. Only one agent-detection helper remains in the Python source.

## Out of scope

- The E-1803 PostToolUse nudge (user decision).
- A `--global` output style install; E-1919's project-scoped decision stands. If the
  per-project activation proves too narrow across 50+ sessions, that is a separate
  change against E-1785, not this task.
- Any enforcement gate. This task delivers instructions on three surfaces plus one
  human-facing FYI; it deliberately adds no teeth.

# Plan — E-1915: refuse to remove a task that still has relations

`task remove` orphans `task_deps` rows, and reused ids resurrect them. The fix is
a guard, not a cascade.

## The decision: deny on all six, no exemptions

`task remove` REFUSES while any `task_deps` row references the task, and names
the rows so the operator can clear them. It does not delete relations as a side
effect of deleting a task.

Deny rather than cascade because a severed relation is unrecoverable and a
refusal costs one command. Cascading can be revisited if the friction proves
real; the reverse migration (discovering months later that a chain was silently
severed) has no fix.

All six types, including `relates_to`, with no per-type exemption. `relates_to`
is the weakest relation and was the obvious candidate to auto-delete, but one
rule that always holds beats two rules with a judgment call at the boundary —
and every "harmless" exemption is a second code path that can orphan rows again.
It is one `task unlink` away. If it proves annoying in practice, relax that one
type then, with evidence.

This matches what `task remove` already does with children: it RAISES (not
warns) and tells you to pass `--cascade`. Refusing on relations is the existing
shape, not a new kind of behavior.

## No new flag. `--cascade` below is the one that already exists

`endless task remove` already has `--cascade` ("Also remove all descendants"). It
is about CHILDREN and predates this task. Nothing here adds a relations
equivalent — there is deliberately no way to remove a task and its relations in
one command, because that is the cascade this plan rejects.

It is named below only to settle WHICH tasks get checked:

- `task remove E-100` deletes one task — check E-100's relations.
- `task remove E-100 --cascade` deletes E-100 and every descendant — check all of
  their relations too.

The second case is not a nicety. If only the root were checked, the guard would
be bypassed by removing a parent instead of the child that holds the link, and
the descendants would be deleted with their relations orphaned exactly as today.

## Implementation

`remove_item` in `src/endless/task_cmd.py` (currently ~line 2260).

1. After the existing child-count check, collect the relation rows for every id
   about to be deleted:

   - Without `--cascade`, that is the one task.
   - With `--cascade`, that is the task PLUS its full descendant set. Reuse the
     `WITH RECURSIVE tree(id)` query already in the function (it is computed
     today only to print a count). This is the case most likely to have
     relations, and checking only the root would let a parent removal bypass the
     guard entirely.

   ```sql
   SELECT id, source_id, target_id, dep_type FROM task_deps
    WHERE (source_type = 'task' AND source_id  IN (<ids>))
       OR (target_type = 'task' AND target_id IN (<ids>))
    ORDER BY id
   ```

2. If any row comes back, raise `click.ClickException` listing each relation as
   the exact `task unlink` command that clears it, using the CANONICAL_DEP_TYPES
   display name and the correct source/target order:

   ```
   Task E-1914 has 3 relations. Removing it would orphan them —
   task_deps rows survive a task delete, and ids are reused, so a later
   task inheriting E-1914 would inherit these too. Unlink them first:

       endless task unlink 1914 --to 1911 --type cleans_up
       endless task unlink 1914 --to 1900 --type relates_to
       endless task unlink 1899 --to 1914 --type blocks
   ```

   Under `--cascade`, attribute each row to the descendant it belongs to, or the
   operator cannot tell which of several tasks is holding up the removal.

3. Raise BEFORE `emit_event(kind="task.deleted", ...)`. That event currently
   fires ahead of the delete; a refusal after it would publish a deletion that
   never happened.

## Also fix: the rows already orphaned

The guard stops new orphans; it does not clean up the ones the ledger has
accumulated. Add a repair that reports and deletes rows whose task endpoint no
longer exists:

```sql
SELECT * FROM task_deps
 WHERE (source_type = 'task' AND source_id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM tasks))
    OR (target_type = 'task' AND target_id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM tasks))
```

Fold it into whatever `endless reconcile` already does for consistency repair
rather than adding a new verb. Print what it removed — a silent repair of silent
corruption teaches nothing.

Note the ordering hazard: this query only finds orphans whose id is still FREE.
Any orphan whose id has already been reused is indistinguishable from a genuine
relation and cannot be recovered by query. Run the repair as part of landing
this, and accept that anything already resurrected is lost.

## Audit in the same pass

Every other table keyed on a task id has the same reuse exposure and should be
checked for the same gap — `task_landings` and `session_task_relations` at
minimum. Report what is found; fix in this task only if the fix is small,
otherwise file it.

## Verification — `tests/tasks/e-1915-verify.sh`

- Removing a task with a `blocks` relation is refused, and the message contains
  the exact `task unlink` command that clears it.
- Refused for each of the six types independently, `relates_to` included — the
  no-exemption rule is the decision, so it is the assertion.
- Refused when the task is the TARGET as well as the source (the `1899 blocks
  1914` direction), which is the half a naive `source_id = ?` check misses.
- `--cascade` is refused when a DESCENDANT holds the relation and the root holds
  none, and the message names the descendant.
- After `task unlink`, the same removal succeeds and leaves zero `task_deps`
  rows referencing the id.
- The reconcile repair deletes a hand-seeded orphan row and reports it.
- Regression: removing a task with no relations still works, and removing a task
  with children still raises the existing `--cascade` message.

# Second landing — folding in E-1927 and E-1928

Both were found while verifying the first landing and filed as follow-ups. Both
are folded back in here rather than tracked separately: neither needed a design
call once stated, and both reuse helpers the first landing already added.

## E-1927 — the other way a task gets deleted

The first landing put the guard in `remove_item`, so it only covered
`endless task remove`. Two commands delete `tasks` rows without going near it:

- `endless task import <file> --replace` → `_do_import` (`task_cmd.py`)
- `endless task import-json --clear`     → `import_json` (`task_cmd.py`)

Both emit `task.bulk_cleared`, which `execTaskBulkCleared`
(`internal/events/executor.go`) runs as
`DELETE FROM tasks WHERE project_id = ? AND source_file = ?` — no relation
cleanup, no guard. Reproduced before the fix: import a plan, link one of its
tasks, re-import with `--replace` — task gone, `task_deps` row still there.

**Decision: same rule, same refusal.** The reason to hesitate was that refusing
a *bulk file refresh* is more obstructive than refusing one named `task remove`
— the operator may not know which relation the guard means. That is answered by
the message rather than by a weaker rule: it names the file, groups every row
under the task holding it, and gives the exact `unlink`. An imported task that
has since been linked to is not disposable just because a file regenerated it,
and the relation is unrecoverable however the task went away.

No new flag. Re-import without `--replace` / `--clear` if the refresh matters
more than the relation.

Implementation: `_refuse_bulk_clear_with_relations(project_id, source_file)`
resolves the tasks that clear would delete and hands them to the existing
`_relations_referencing()`. Raised before the emit, like the remove-side guard.
The message body is now shared — `_orphan_refusal()` builds it for both call
sites, so the rule reads identically however the caller got here.

## E-1928 — `--cascade` always reported 0 descendants

Pre-existing, not introduced by the first landing; found while verifying the
cascade guard. `remove_item` emitted `task.deleted` and only THEN ran a
recursive query to count the descendants it had just deleted. `emit_event`
executes the delete synchronously, so the CTE always seeded from an empty table:

    $ endless task remove 8600 --cascade      # parent + child + grandchild
    • Removed E-8600 and 0 descendant(s): P

Fix: `_removal_id_set(item_id, cascade)` — added by the first landing for the
guard — already computes exactly that id set, before the delete. `remove_item`
now calls it once, passes it to the guard, and reports `len(removal_ids) - 1`.
The post-delete query is gone; no query was added to replace it.

## Verification — the same `tests/tasks/e-1915-verify.sh`

Folded in as new checks rather than a second script:

- Section E gains an assertion that the cascade success line reports the real
  descendant count (`and 2 descendant(s)`), not 0.
- New section E2: a re-import with `--replace` is refused while an imported
  task holds a relation; the message names the file and the clearing command;
  the task and its relation both survive the refusal; after `unlink` the same
  re-import succeeds and leaves nothing orphaned; a relation on a task the
  import does not own never blocks the refresh.
- `tests/test_task_remove_relations.py` gains unit coverage for
  `_refuse_bulk_clear_with_relations` (per-file scoping, multi-task
  attribution, the `json_import` pseudo-source) and for `_removal_id_set`
  returning the whole subtree.

## Still open — E-1926 only

The FK-free tables (`session_tasks`, `session_hidden_tasks`, `session_notices`,
`project_next_tasks` / `_pending`) stay out. They are not relations, there is no
`unlink` to demand, and their schema comments say outliving the task is the
point — so the guard would be unclearable rather than merely strict. That needs
a decision about what a freed task id means, which is E-1926's job.

fields.outcome: Folded into E-1915's second landing rather than tracked separately — the guard is the same rule at a second call site (_refuse_bulk_clear_with_relations), and reuses _relations_referencing() from the first landing. `task import --replace` and `import-json --clear` now refuse while a relation references any task they would delete. No design call was needed: the objection (a bulk refresh refusing is more obstructive than one named removal) is answered by the message naming the file and the exact unlink, not by a weaker rule.

Folded into E-1915's second landing. Three-line fix reusing _removal_id_set() from the first landing: remove_item now computes the removal id set once before the emit and reports len(ids)-1, replacing the recursive query that ran after emit_event (which deletes the subtree synchronously) and so always counted 0.

# Plan — E-1893: require replies to restate the task IDs they are about

## Decisions (user, 2026-08-08)

Delivery surfaces: **handoff templates, the E-1919 output style, and `endless guide`**.
Explicitly NOT the E-1803 PostToolUse nudge — E-1911 just rewrote that nudge and parked
E-1901's enforcement arm, so it is recently-settled ground this task will not disturb.

The style's reach gap is closed two ways: activate it for endless now, and add a
**dim FYI on stderr** telling a *human* operator the style is installed but inactive.
Optional in principle; treated as required for any project using Endless for now.

## Part 1 — handoff templates (one sentence, one place)

The analysis's open question (a line in each of seven templates vs a shared fragment)
resolves itself: `internal/templatecmd/templates/handoff/_close.tmpl` already exists,
already holds the reporting instructions, and is already parsed into every handoff
template's set via `handoffPartialNames`. Add the rule to the `handoff_close` define.

Wording must cover the crux from the analysis — the subject is often NOT the session's
own task, so the tmux window title does not supply the missing ID:

> Name the explicit task ID(s) in the first sentence that makes a claim about a task —
> including tasks other than your own, where my window title tells me nothing.

Do NOT add it to `handoff_verify` / `handoff_nonverify`; those are about the verify
command, and duplicating the rule invites drift between copies.

## Part 2 — E-1919 output style

The style's `## Lead with the IDs` section already says to open with the bare
identifiers the answer concerns. It does not stress the other-tasks case, which the
analysis calls the crux. Strengthen that section only — do not restructure it.

Because the style file is embedded, the change is made in
`internal/outputstylecmd/templates/Endless.md.tmpl`, then re-materialized into
`.claude/output-styles/Endless.md` with `outputstyle install --force`. Both copies must
be committed; a stale committed copy would silently shadow the intent.

`tests/tasks/e-1919-verify.sh` section 8 asserts the style body's contract clauses. Add
an assertion for the other-tasks wording so this cannot regress.

## Part 3 — `endless guide`

Add the rule to the reporting guidance in the guide's orchestration/reporting section,
for sessions not started from a handoff. Keep it to the same one sentence used in
`_close.tmpl` — three surfaces carrying three paraphrases is how the rule drifts.

Re-run `just regenerate-guide` if the section map changes.

## Part 4 — activate the style for endless

Commit `"outputStyle": "Endless"` into the main checkout's tracked
`.claude/settings.json`. Verified safe: `just claude-settings-init` rebuilds each
worktree's settings from the committed copy's non-hook keys plus the working copy's,
replacing only `hooks` (justfile:381-385), so the key survives worktree regeneration
rather than being dropped.

Note this is a genuine behavior change for every endless session, which is why E-1919
made it opt-in. It is being opted into deliberately here, not by default.

## Part 5 — the dim FYI (human-only, stderr, appended)

**Trigger:** any `endless` command run by a human. Never when run by an agent.

**Detection already exists — twice.** `agent_help.is_claude_code_agent()` and
`task_cmd._running_under_agent()` are byte-identical (`CLAUDECODE == "1"`). Consolidate
onto `agent_help.is_claude_code_agent()` and delete the duplicate rather than adding a
third caller — same reasoning that folded `templatecmd` onto
`monitor.ProjectRootFromCwd` in E-1919.

**Behavior:**
- Fires only when `not is_claude_code_agent()`.
- Fires only when the project has the style file present but `outputStyle` unset (or set
  to something else) in `.claude/settings.json` — i.e. exactly the inert state
  `outputstyle install` warns about.
- Writes to **stderr**, dim, appended after the command's normal output, so it never
  corrupts stdout for pipes/`--json` consumers.
- One line. Not an error, not a non-zero exit.
- Suppressed when the project has no style file at all (nothing to activate) and when
  `.claude/settings.json` is unreadable.

**Wording:** dim, and it must name the activation route, since there is no
`/output-style` command:

> FYI: the Endless output style is installed but not active — `/config output-style=Endless`

**Throttle — mtime marker, not the DB.** An earlier draft of this plan said to reuse
`monitor.ShouldThrottle`. That is wrong: it is Go-side and DB-backed (queries the
`activity` table), so calling it from the Python CLI would mean a subprocess on every
`endless` invocation — unacceptable overhead for a one-line FYI. Python's
`task_cmd._bg_throttle_warn` is a *count* threshold, not a time throttle, so it is not
the shape either.

Use a marker file instead: `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/endless/outputstyle-fyi/<project>.stamp`.
Print only when the marker is absent or older than the interval, then touch it. No DB,
no subprocess, ~5 lines. Default interval 4 hours, overridable via
`.endless/config.json`. A missing/unwritable cache dir means print (fail open) —
suppressing the reminder silently is the worse failure.

Do NOT ship an unthrottled per-invocation nag; that is the noise that got E-1901's gate
parked.

**Placement:** a single hook in the Python CLI's result callback / group teardown so it
appends after any subcommand, rather than being pasted into individual commands.

## Verification

Fold into the existing suite per the one-command rule:
`esu && ./tests/tasks/e-1893-verify.sh`

Checks:
1. `handoff_close` renders the ID rule for every handoff type (todo, bugfix, research,
   epic, brainstorm, respawn) — asserts the shared partial actually reaches all of them.
2. The rule appears exactly once per rendered handoff, not once per template that
   includes a partial.
3. The style body carries the other-tasks wording.
4. The embedded template and the committed `.claude/output-styles/Endless.md` are
   byte-identical — catches a re-materialization that was forgotten.
5. `endless guide` output contains the rule.
6. The FYI fires with `CLAUDECODE` unset and a project in the inert state.
7. The FYI does NOT fire when `CLAUDECODE=1`.
8. The FYI does NOT fire when `outputStyle` is already `Endless`.
9. The FYI goes to stderr, not stdout: stdout of a `--json` command still parses.
10. The FYI does not change exit status.
11. Only one agent-detection helper remains in the Python source.

## Out of scope

- The E-1803 PostToolUse nudge (user decision).
- A `--global` output style install; E-1919's project-scoped decision stands. If the
  per-project activation proves too narrow across 50+ sessions, that is a separate
  change against E-1785, not this task.
- Any enforcement gate. This task delivers instructions on three surfaces plus one
  human-facing FYI; it deliberately adds no teeth.

payload.title: Orphaned relation rows are prevented by refusing the delete, not by cascading it
payload.description: task_deps and decision_relations carry no foreign key on their task endpoint — SQLite cannot express an FK whose target table varies by row — so a task delete leaves its relation rows behind, and reused task ids resurrect them as computed fact (E-1911's report claimed an unrelated E-1914 as a follow-up it filed). Enforce in application code, by REFUSING the delete and naming the unlink that clears each row. Deny rather than cascade: a severed relation is unrecoverable, a refusal costs one command. No per-type exemption — relates_to included; one rule that always holds beats a judgment call at the boundary. The guard belongs at every task-deleting verb, not only the one that prompted it: task remove was guarded first, and task import --replace was found orphaning rows the same way. reconcile() also repairs already-orphaned rows, but only while the freed id is unused — which is why prevention is primary. Governs relation rows only; the FK-free history tables are E-1926's question.

# Problem

Endless mints monotonic E-NNN IDs from a single local counter. Two developers filing concurrently both mint the same next number, so ledgers collide on merge. A distributed-safe identifier scheme is required before two people can share a project through git.

# Candidate approaches (to explore, not yet rank)

## 1. Human-initials suffix
Append a per-developer suffix to the number, e.g. E-123-abc vs E-123-xyz.
- Each developer omits their own suffix when typing their own IDs but must type others' suffixes.
- Cheap; no new infrastructure. Cost: humans type and remember initials; the suffix namespace is manually managed.

## 2. Content-hash paired identifier (already filed as E-816)
A local human-friendly id plus a content-hash global id (SHA-256 prefix), mapped one-to-one in the projection; cross-repo deps use the global id.
- Git-hash-like; no coordination needed. Cost: global ids are not human-memorable; needs a stable local-to-global mapping story on merge.

## 3. Central ID-dispensing service
A pluggable CreateTaskId service hands out globally-unique ids on demand.
- A subset of the pluggable Task-backend service (E-800). Removes collisions by coordination. Cost: requires availability of the service; offline filing needs a fallback.

## 4. Git-as-CAS dispenser (added from E-1926, 2026-08-09)
Use the team's existing git remote as the coordination primitive instead of standing up a service. To mint an id: read the id file from a dedicated repo or Gist, increment it, commit, and push. A successful push IS the allocation; a rejected (non-fast-forward) push means someone else took that number, so pull, take the next one, and retry. Classic compare-and-swap, with the git host providing the serialization.

- Zero new infrastructure — no service to write, deploy, host, or keep up.
- Availability equals the availability of the git host the team already cannot work without, which answers the "what if the dispenser is down" objection against #3 (if GitHub is down, the team is not collaborating anyway).
- Ids stay short bare integers — nothing extra to type, unlike #1 and #2.
- Self-hostable end to end: an open-source user's provider can be their own LAN git server.
- Cost: latency is a push round-trip per `task add` (acceptable — this is an interactive command), and contention retries grow with team size, though a team small enough to share one Endless project will not contend meaningfully.
- Same shape as #3 from the caller's side: both are just an `allocate()` behind the pluggable provider interface, so choosing #4 does not preclude adding #3 later. #4 is arguably the reference implementation of #3 that ships without a server.

# Constraints any candidate must satisfy

## No id is ever reused (from E-1926, locked 2026-08-09)
A freed id that can be re-minted reintroduces the whole orphaned-row bug class: FK-free rows keyed on a task id (`session_tasks`, `session_hidden_tasks`, `session_notices`, `project_next_tasks`/`_pending`) deliberately outlive their task, and a reused id makes them resurrect against unrelated work. E-1915 hit this for `task_deps`; E-1926 found four more tables and settled the policy: **no entity id is ever reused, for any entity type.** Whatever scheme wins here must make re-minting a spent id impossible, not merely unlikely. Gaps in the sequence are legal and permanent.

## An id is spent by the ledger, not by the table (from E-1926)
The SQLite DB is a projection rebuilt from `.endless/db-ledger/*.jsonl`. Allocation that reads only the live projection will re-free ids across a rebuild unless every removal is materialized as a tombstone the rebuild replays. Any scheme that mints from local state must therefore mint against the append-only record's high-water mark, not against `MAX(id)` over live rows. (Coordination-based schemes #3 and #4 sidestep this — the dispenser is itself the high-water mark.)

# Cross-links

- E-816 is the concrete content-hash option.
- E-800 is the pluggable task-backend feature; the central dispenser is a subset of it.
- E-1032 (E-NNN to ET-NNN prefix migration) and E-1123 (session-worktree branch collisions) are adjacent ID concerns to keep consistent with whatever is chosen.
- E-1926 settled the no-reuse policy and the tombstone mechanism that enforces it locally; it is the source of the two constraints above.

# Settled adjacent question: no cross-entity unification

E-1926 considered and rejected a universal id space in which tasks, sessions and decisions all draw from one sequence (so `12345` would be unambiguous and `E-12345` would preclude `ES-12345`). Rejected because (a) external providers cannot honor it — JIRA namespaces per project, GitHub shares one sequence between issues and PRs only — so the guarantee would evaporate exactly where the pluggable-provider roadmap leads; (b) sessions are the highest-volume entity and would inflate the scarce short-id space that both task and session ids are typed from by hand; and (c) ids are already embedded in immutable artifacts (commit subjects, branch names, worktree and sandbox paths, and the prose of every plan and ledger entry), so renumbering would make history lie. Per-entity-type id spaces stay, and the `E-`/`ES-`/`ED-` prefix remains part of the identity rather than display sugar.

# Output

A recommended identifier scheme with enough detail to file the implementation task(s) that unblock the two-developer milestone.

payload.description: Once an id is dispensed it is spent, used or not — for tasks, sessions, decisions, and any entity added later. payload.description: A single universal sequence shared by tasks, sessions and decisions (so a bare 12345 would be unambiguous and E-12345 would preclude ES-12345) was considered and rejected. payload.title: Make task removal set removed=1 instead of deleting, and filter removed rows from every read path
payload.description: Per ED-1547. 'task remove' retains the row and sets a new removed flag on tasks rather than issuing a DELETE, so the id can never be re-minted. The bulk of the work is the read-path audit: queries that today drop dangling references via inner join (session_status.go in internal monitor, lines 184, 349 and 480, among them) will start matching the retained row, so every read path — CLI listings, session status, the monitor, session next, the web dashboard, and the four FK-free consumers session_tasks, session_hidden_tasks, session_notices and project_next_tasks plus _pending — must filter on removed. A missed filter leaks a removed task into a listing. Also confirm the db-ledger projector replays a removal as a retained removed=1 row, since replaying it as a real delete would re-free the id across a rebuild.

payload.title: Extend the never-reuse-an-id policy to every non-task entity with a delete path
payload.description: Per ED-1547, no entity id is ever reused, for any entity type — not just tasks. Audit every delete path in the schema and the CLI for entities that mint ids (sessions, decisions, verbs, notes, projects, and anything else) and convert each hard delete to the retained removed=1 form, or establish that the entity has no delete path at all. Sessions are the known live exposure: session_tasks.session_id is FK-free in exactly the way task_id is, task_cmd already renders a state for a touch whose session row is gone, and the dead-pane reaper work in E-1898 is in that neighborhood. payload.title: Drop pending session_notices undelivered when their task is removed
payload.description: Per ED-1547, this is the one exception to the filter-everywhere rule for removed rows. An undelivered notice about a removed task is dead mail: filtering it on read leaves it in the queue permanently, so removal deletes the pending notice rows instead. Scope is only notices still pending delivery — already-delivered notice history is unaffected. Depends on the removed flag existing (E-1929).

payload.title: Purge FK-free rows already resurrected against a reused task id

Sweep the four tables on that comparison and delete the matches, then decide whether the check earns a permanent home in the E-1915 reconcile repair or is a one-shot migration. # E-1926 — What FK-free task-keyed rows do when a task id is freed and reused

## The answer

They stay attached to the id, and the id is never freed.

The question as filed assumed the id would be reused and asked what the four
tables should do about it. The requester rejected the premise outright: id reuse
is the defect, not the condition to design around. Once an id is spent it stays
spent, so a row that outlives its task points at a retired number forever —
which is exactly what the four schema comments ("the row must outlive its task")
always claimed would happen. Non-reuse does not paper over the bug; it makes
those comments true instead of aspirational.

This dissolves the per-table design call the task was filed to make. There is no
policy to choose for `session_tasks` vs `session_hidden_tasks` vs
`session_notices` vs `project_next_tasks`/`_pending`. There is one id-lifecycle
fix and a read-path audit behind it.

Recorded as **ED-1547** (no reuse, removal keeps the row) and **ED-1548** (no
universal cross-entity id).

## What was decided

**No entity id is ever reused — any entity type, not just tasks.** Dispensed
means spent, used or not. Gaps are legal and permanent, and nothing may assume
ids are dense or contiguous.

**Removal keeps the row and sets `removed=1`.** `task remove` stops issuing a
DELETE. Retaining the row makes re-minting impossible by construction rather
than by convention.

A separate spent-ids table was considered and rejected: a second table holding
the ids that another table needs has too much potential to drift from it.
Keeping the row keeps the fact in one place.

**Removed rows never render.** This is the uniform rule for all four tables and
everywhere else, and it is where the actual work is. The reads in
`session_status.go` (lines 184, 349, 480) inner-join `tasks`, so today a row
whose task was deleted silently drops out — correct behavior, obtained by
accident. Retaining the row makes those joins start matching, so the fix
*introduces* a leak unless every read path filters on `removed`. That filter is
the ongoing cost of this decision and it is re-payable by every query written
from here on.

**One exception: pending `session_notices` are dropped, not filtered.** An
undelivered notice about a removed task is dead mail. Filtering it on read
leaves it in the queue permanently; deleting it is the honest disposal. Scope is
rows with `notified = 0` only.

**An id is spent by the ledger, not by the table.** The SQLite DB is a
projection of `.endless/db-ledger/*.jsonl`; the `removed=1` row is the
projection's materialization of a fact the ledger already holds permanently, in
the create and remove events. The rebuild must replay removal as a retained
`removed=1` row. If it ever replayed removal as a real delete, a rebuild would
re-free the id and reuse would return on a path nobody would think to test. This
holds only while ledger compaction stays out of scope — ruled out for the
foreseeable future, since dropping create events would require finding and
fixing every reference to those ids in all content.

## What was rejected

**A universal id space** shared by tasks, sessions and decisions, such that
`12345` is unambiguous and `E-12345` precludes `ES-12345`. Raised by the
requester and rejected on three grounds: pluggable ID providers cannot honor it
(JIRA namespaces per project; GitHub shares one sequence between issues and PRs
and nothing else), so the guarantee would evaporate exactly where the E-800 /
E-1831 roadmap leads; sessions are the highest-volume entity and would inflate
the short-id space that both task and session ids are typed from by hand; and
ids are already embedded in immutable artifacts — commit subjects, branch names,
worktree and sandbox paths, and the prose of every plan and ledger entry — so
renumbering would make history lie while not renumbering would leave a permanent
split regime. Full rationale in ED-1548.

**Splitting storage identity from display identity** — an internal never-reused
integer for joins, with the human-facing id a separate, possibly delegated
concern. Proposed during the session and rejected by the requester with the
decisive argument: agents write ids into plans, ledger entries and commit
messages constantly, so the id in prose *is* the identity. On a team, a
locally-minted `E-1926` names one developer's task and not their teammate's, and
no amount of internal cleanliness fixes that. This is a real requirement, it is
about cross-*developer* uniqueness rather than cross-*entity* uniqueness, and it
belongs to E-1831 — not here.

**Block allocation as an availability hedge** for a remote ID provider. Raised
and dismissed as YAGNI: Endless is open source, a team's provider will almost
certainly be a service they control (possibly on their own LAN), and the
failure mode is not worth designing against before it appears.

## What went upstream to E-1831

E-1831 ("Choose a collision-free distributed task-ID scheme") is the home for
distributed ids and is still `submitted`, not answered. Three things from this
session were written into its plan text rather than duplicated here:

**A fourth candidate — git-as-CAS dispenser.** The requester's idea: to mint an
id, read the id file from a dedicated repo or Gist, increment, commit, push. A
successful push *is* the allocation; a rejected non-fast-forward push means
someone else took that number, so pull, take the next, retry. Compare-and-swap
with the git host providing serialization. Zero new infrastructure, availability
equal to the git host the team already cannot work without, ids stay short bare
integers, and it is self-hostable end to end. Same shape as candidate #3 from
the caller's side — both are an `allocate()` behind the provider interface — so
it is arguably the reference implementation of #3 that ships without a server.

**Two constraints every candidate must satisfy:** no scheme may permit
re-minting a spent id, and any scheme minting from local state must mint against
the ledger high-water mark rather than `MAX(id)` over live rows.

**A note that cross-entity unification is settled and rejected**, so E-1831 does
not reopen it.

## Follow-ups filed

- **E-1929** — Make task removal set `removed=1` instead of deleting, and filter
  removed rows from every read path. The core implementation, including the
  projector/rebuild check.
- **E-1930** — Extend the never-reuse-an-id policy to every non-task entity with
  a delete path. Sessions are the known live exposure: `session_tasks.session_id`
  is FK-free in exactly the way `task_id` is.
- **E-1931** — Drop pending `session_notices` undelivered when their task is
  removed. Blocked by E-1929.
- **E-1932** — Purge FK-free rows already resurrected against a reused id. The
  policy is prospective, so pre-existing damage stays wrong; it is detectable
  because all four tables carry a timestamp (`created_at`, `hidden_at`,
  `changed_at`, `added_at`), and a row predating `tasks.created_at` of the id's
  current occupant provably belongs to a previous occupant.

## Measured, not inferred

Carried forward from the task's analysis: after `endless task remove 8001` in an
isolated DB, `session_tasks` held 2 rows for 8001, `session_hidden_tasks` 1,
`session_notices` 1, `project_next_tasks` 1. For contrast `task_landings` (FK ON
DELETE CASCADE), `sessions.active_task_id` and `session_statuses.active_task_id`
(FK ON DELETE SET NULL) all cleared correctly, and `session_task_relations` is
the relation-kind vocabulary table, not task-keyed at all.

Confirmed this session: all four tables carry a timestamp column, which is what
makes E-1932's detector possible; `session_notices.notified` is the pending flag
that scopes E-1931; and `project_next_tasks.task_id` is TEXT where the other
three are INTEGER, so any cross-table sweep needs a cast.

`docs/guide/orchestration.md` ("A verify suite is a land-time gate, not a
standing regression suite") states three prohibitions:

- Don't run another task's already-landed verify suite.
- Don't edit a landed task's verify suite.
- Coverage that must survive belongs in the project's own test suite.

The rule is documented and was still violated three times in one session
(E-1901), including by a session whose handoff explicitly named
`endless guide orchestration`. It was then violated twice more in E-1889, by a
session that had read the same principle in its own task's analysis field on
its first tool call. Documentation is the wrong layer: a rule that must be read
gets skipped, and the skip does not feel like a violation — running an existing,
runnable-looking script feels like diligence.

Put the enforcement where the act happens, in `internal/hookcmd/claude.go`,
following the `blockPlanFileWriteIfApplicable` precedent already in that file
(same shape, same class of problem: a path that must not be hand-edited).

## Both suite forms, from day one

A suite exists in two forms and the guard must know both, or it goes blind
exactly when the project migrates:

| Form | Path | Run by |
|------|------|--------|
| script (current) | `tests/tasks/e-<n>-verify.sh` | `./tests/tasks/e-<n>-verify.sh` |
| manifest (settled destination) | `.endless/tasks/E-<n>/verify.toml` | `endless task verify <id>` |

Note the casing differs — the script form is lowercase `e-1758-verify.sh`, the
manifest directory is uppercase `E-1758` (verified against the two manifests
that exist today, `.endless/tasks/E-1603/` and `.endless/tasks/E-1758/`). The
id-extraction predicate must accept either and must not be case-brittle.

Building the manifest arm now is not speculation. Two manifests already exist,
`endless task verify` already discovers and runs them, and the guide already
names `.endless/tasks/<id>/verify.toml` as the settled form. Shipping a
script-only guard would mean re-opening this task the moment the migration
lands — the precise failure mode this task exists to prevent.

### What must NOT be blocked

- **`.endless/verify.toml` at the project root.** Same filename, one level up,
  and it is not a per-task suite — it carries shared `setup`/`teardown`/`seed`/
  `needs` composing beneath every task manifest. The predicate keys on the
  `.endless/tasks/<id>/` segment, not on the basename.
- **The tests a manifest points AT.** A manifest is a pointer, never a
  re-description: its `[[check]]` entries select native `gotest`/`pytest` tests
  living in `internal/...` and `tests/...`. Those are the project's durable
  suite and must stay freely editable forever. Blocking the manifest must not
  leak into blocking what it names — which is the whole reason the durable-test
  half of the prohibition works.

## Arm 1 — refuse the EDIT (the more damaging violation)

`PreToolUse` on Write/Edit/NotebookEdit: refuse a target matching either suite
form when task NNNN has landed AND is not this session's active task.

This is the arm that matters most. In E-1901 the suites were edited via Edit
without ever being run, so any guard living inside the script itself was inert.
Retrofitting the target string of a landed suite rewrites the record of what was
true when that task landed. In E-1889 the motive was more specific and worth
naming, because it will recur: the session's own change broke a landed suite's
assertion, and it edited the suite to keep it green. That is the failure this
arm must catch — the edit feels like fixing a break, not like falsifying a
record.

## Arm 2 — refuse the RUN

Same handler, Bash tool. Two invocation shapes, both refused for a landed,
non-active task:

- direct execution of `tests/tasks/e-<n>-verify.sh` (any of `./x`, `bash x`,
  `sh x`, an absolute path);
- the manifest runner: `endless task verify <id>`, plus the `just verify <id>`
  wrapper that forwards to it.

The bare `endless task verify` with no id resolves to the session's own active
task and is always allowed — that is the pre-land gate doing its job.

A failure from a landed suite is meaningless by design, and acting on one
produces exactly the non-problem work E-1909 and E-1910 were (both declined).

## Landed-ness test

`session-query task-report --id N` already returns a `landed` bool; reuse it
rather than adding a second notion of landed-ness. Carve out the session's own
active task so the live, pre-land gate still runs and can still be authored.

A reopened task (`revisit`, per E-1889) is once again the session's active task,
so the carve-out restores its suite to writable and runnable without a special
case — reopening genuinely does put the task back in its pre-land window.

## Why no directory move, and no per-script retrofit

Moving `tests/tasks/` → `verify/tasks/` was considered and rejected: 123 task
rows and 141 commit messages embed the current path, all of them immutable
records, and `.endless/tasks/<id>/verify.toml` is already the settled
destination as the runner matures — a move would churn the script form on its
way out. A rename also would not have prevented the violation: the scripts were
run because they existed and looked runnable, not because of the directory name.

Because the guard lives in the hook, NO existing suite is touched and every
landed suite of either form is covered the moment it ships. That is the point: a
per-script guard could only be added by editing landed suites, which is the
prohibition itself.

## Honest limits

- This cannot stop an agent from FILING a task about a landed suite — that is a
  judgment call no path pattern catches. E-1909/E-1910's decline reasons are the
  record for that case.
- It cannot stop a run laundered through an indirection the Bash matcher does
  not see (a wrapper script, `xargs`, a shell function). Arm 2 is a guardrail
  against the reflex, not a sandbox; Arm 1 is the arm that must be airtight.

## Verification

Unit tests on the pure predicate, covering both forms:

- path regex matches `tests/tasks/e-<n>-verify.sh` and
  `.endless/tasks/E-<n>/verify.toml`, in either casing, and not their
  neighbours;
- the project-root `.endless/verify.toml` is NOT matched;
- a path named by a manifest's `[[check]]` (e.g. `internal/monitor/x_test.go`)
  is NOT matched;
- landed + non-active → block; landed + active → allow; unlanded → allow;

fields.analysis:
Absorbs E-1930 (extend the policy to non-task entities) and E-1931 (drop pending
notices), both closed obsolete in favour of this task.

## Scope: which entities are covered

ED-1547 covers any id that something outside its own row refers to — logically,
not only where SQLite declares a FOREIGN KEY. That is tasks, sessions and
decisions. A junction or child table whose surrogate primary key nothing else
stores and nobody types stays an unrestricted hard delete.

## Three parts

**1. Convert each covered entity's delete path.** Set a new `removed` flag on the
row rather than issuing a DELETE. Sessions are the known live exposure:
`session_tasks.session_id` refers to a session with no declared constraint,
exactly as `task_id` does, and `task_cmd.py` already renders a state for a touch
whose session row is gone — useful precedent for the mirror case.

**2. The read-path audit — the bulk of the work.** Queries that today drop
dangling references via inner join will start matching the retained row, so a
removed entity leaks into listings unless each read filters on `removed`. Known
sites include `session_status.go` in internal monitor at lines 184, 349 and 480.
The full sweep covers CLI listings, session status, the monitor, `session next`,
the web dashboard, and the four consumers `session_tasks`,
`session_hidden_tasks`, `session_notices` and `project_next_tasks`/`_pending`.

**3. Drop pending notices in the same removal path.** Delete `session_notices`
rows with `notified = 0` for the removed task rather than filtering them —
an undelivered notice about a removed task is dead mail that would otherwise sit
in the queue permanently. Delivered notice history is unaffected. This is not an
exception to the id rule: a notice's own id is an internal row handle nobody
holds.

## Rebuild check

Confirm the db-ledger projector replays a removal as a retained `removed=1` row.
If it ever replayed removal as a real delete, a rebuild would re-free the id and
reuse would return on a path nobody would think to test.

fields.outcome:
# E-1926 — What FK-free task-keyed rows do when a task id is freed and reused

## The answer

They stay attached to the id, and the id is never freed.

The question as filed assumed the id would be reused and asked what the four
tables should do about it. The requester rejected the premise outright: id reuse
is the defect, not the condition to design around. Once an id is spent it stays
spent, so a row that outlives its task points at a retired number forever —
which is exactly what the four schema comments ("the row must outlive its task")
always claimed would happen. Non-reuse does not paper over the bug; it makes
those comments true instead of aspirational.

This dissolves the per-table design call the task was filed to make. There is no
policy to choose for `session_tasks` vs `session_hidden_tasks` vs
`session_notices` vs `project_next_tasks`/`_pending`. There is one id-lifecycle
fix and a read-path audit behind it.

Recorded as **ED-1547** (no reuse, removal keeps the row) and **ED-1548** (no
universal cross-entity id).

## What was decided

**No id that anything else refers to is ever reused.** Dispensed means spent,
used or not. Gaps are legal and permanent, and nothing may assume ids are dense
or contiguous.

"Refers to" means stored in another table — logically, not only where SQLite
declares a `FOREIGN KEY` — or handled by a human or agent: typed, or written
into a plan, commit subject, branch name, or path. That covers tasks, sessions
and decisions. An id that is a purely internal row handle, a surrogate primary
key nothing else stores and nobody types, may be reused freely, so junction and
child tables keep unrestricted hard deletes.

The rule was first drafted as a flat "no entity id is ever reused" and narrowed
on review. The flat version overreached: it would have bound tables whose ids
nothing holds, for no benefit. Note the declared-constraint test alone would be
insufficient — `session_tasks.task_id` has no `FOREIGN KEY` clause and still
refers to a task, and that reference is the entire bug surface this task was
filed about.

**Removal keeps the row and sets `removed=1`.** `task remove` stops issuing a
DELETE. Retaining the row makes re-minting impossible by construction rather
than by convention.

A separate spent-ids table was considered and rejected: a second table holding
the ids that another table needs has too much potential to drift from it.
Keeping the row keeps the fact in one place.

**Removed rows never render.** This is the uniform rule for all four tables and
everywhere else, and it is where the actual work is. The reads in
`session_status.go` (lines 184, 349, 480) inner-join `tasks`, so today a row
whose task was deleted silently drops out — correct behavior, obtained by
accident. Retaining the row makes those joins start matching, so the fix
*introduces* a leak unless every read path filters on `removed`. That filter is
the ongoing cost of this decision and it is re-payable by every query written
from here on.

**Pending `session_notices` are dropped, not filtered.** An undelivered notice
about a removed task is dead mail. Filtering it on read leaves it in the queue
permanently; deleting it is the honest disposal. Scope is rows with
`notified = 0` only. This is not an exception to the id rule — a notice's own id
is an internal row handle nobody holds, so deleting the row is unrestricted.

**An id is spent by the ledger, not by the table.** The SQLite DB is a
projection of `.endless/db-ledger/*.jsonl`; the `removed=1` row is the
projection's materialization of a fact the ledger already holds permanently, in
the create and remove events. The rebuild must replay removal as a retained
`removed=1` row. If it ever replayed removal as a real delete, a rebuild would
re-free the id and reuse would return on a path nobody would think to test. This
holds only while ledger compaction stays out of scope — ruled out for the
foreseeable future, since dropping create events would require finding and
fixing every reference to those ids in all content.

## What was rejected

**A universal id space** shared by tasks, sessions and decisions, such that
`12345` is unambiguous and `E-12345` precludes `ES-12345`. Raised by the
requester and rejected on three grounds: pluggable ID providers cannot honor it
(JIRA namespaces per project; GitHub shares one sequence between issues and PRs
and nothing else), so the guarantee would evaporate exactly where the E-800 /
E-1831 roadmap leads; sessions are the highest-volume entity and would inflate
the short-id space that both task and session ids are typed from by hand; and
ids are already embedded in immutable artifacts — commit subjects, branch names,
worktree and sandbox paths, and the prose of every plan and ledger entry — so
renumbering would make history lie while not renumbering would leave a permanent
split regime. Full rationale in ED-1548.

**Splitting storage identity from display identity** — an internal never-reused
integer for joins, with the human-facing id a separate, possibly delegated
concern. Proposed during the session and rejected by the requester with the
decisive argument: agents write ids into plans, ledger entries and commit
messages constantly, so the id in prose *is* the identity. On a team, a
locally-minted `E-1926` names one developer's task and not their teammate's, and
no amount of internal cleanliness fixes that. This is a real requirement, it is
about cross-*developer* uniqueness rather than cross-*entity* uniqueness, and it
belongs to E-1831 — not here.

**Block allocation as an availability hedge** for a remote ID provider. Raised
and dismissed as YAGNI: Endless is open source, a team's provider will almost
certainly be a service they control (possibly on their own LAN), and the
failure mode is not worth designing against before it appears.

## What went upstream to E-1831

E-1831 ("Choose a collision-free distributed task-ID scheme") is the home for
distributed ids and is still `submitted`, not answered. Three things from this
session were written into its plan text rather than duplicated here:

**A fourth candidate — git-as-CAS dispenser.** The requester's idea: to mint an
id, read the id file from a dedicated repo or Gist, increment, commit, push. A
successful push *is* the allocation; a rejected non-fast-forward push means
someone else took that number, so pull, take the next, retry. Compare-and-swap
with the git host providing serialization. Zero new infrastructure, availability
equal to the git host the team already cannot work without, ids stay short bare
integers, and it is self-hostable end to end. Same shape as candidate #3 from
the caller's side — both are an `allocate()` behind the provider interface — so
it is arguably the reference implementation of #3 that ships without a server.

**Two constraints every candidate must satisfy:** no scheme may permit
re-minting a spent id, and any scheme minting from local state must mint against
the ledger high-water mark rather than `MAX(id)` over live rows.

**A note that cross-entity unification is settled and rejected**, so E-1831 does
not reopen it.

## Follow-ups filed

Filed as four, merged to two on review. If each task reliably spawns more than
one, the backlog cannot converge, so the split has to earn itself.

- **E-1929** — Replace task, session and decision deletion with a `removed` flag
  filtered from every read path. Covers the schema change for all three covered
  entities, the read-path audit, the pending-notice drop, and the
  projector/rebuild check. Absorbed **E-1930** (extending the policy beyond
  tasks, which the narrowed rule shrank to three known entities) and **E-1931**
  (dropping pending notices, a few lines inside the same removal path). Both
  closed `obsolete`.
- **E-1932** — Purge rows already resurrected against a reused id. The
  policy is prospective, so pre-existing damage stays wrong; it is detectable
  because all four tables carry a timestamp (`created_at`, `hidden_at`,
  `changed_at`, `added_at`), and a row predating `tasks.created_at` of the id's
  current occupant provably belongs to a previous occupant. Kept separate from
  E-1929 because folding a one-shot data repair into a behavior change makes one
  task that can half-fail.

## Measured, not inferred

Carried forward from the task's analysis: after `endless task remove 8001` in an
isolated DB, `session_tasks` held 2 rows for 8001, `session_hidden_tasks` 1,
`session_notices` 1, `project_next_tasks` 1. For contrast `task_landings` (FK ON
DELETE CASCADE), `sessions.active_task_id` and `session_statuses.active_task_id`
(FK ON DELETE SET NULL) all cleared correctly, and `session_task_relations` is
the relation-kind vocabulary table, not task-keyed at all.

Confirmed this session: all four tables carry a timestamp column, which is what
makes E-1932's detector possible; `session_notices.notified` is the pending flag
that scopes E-1931; and `project_next_tasks.task_id` is TEXT where the other
three are INTEGER, so any cross-table sweep needs a cast.
